pr.title: Copy secrets and codes to the clipboard with --clip
pr.head: 969b95a6b5e44cf004565a1d8fc6b11e2513ab31

summary: multipass is a command-line password manager that keeps every secret in one age-encrypted file. Until now, get and otp printed a value to stdout, and the README suggested piping it to pbcopy to copy it. A value copied that way stays on the clipboard until something replaces it, syncs to the user's other Apple devices through Universal Clipboard, and lands in clipboard-history apps.

This pull request adds a --clip flag to get and to otp when it shows a code. With it, multipass writes the value to the macOS clipboard itself, through AppKit's NSPasteboard, and never prints it. It works in three steps:

1. Copy with two markings. The value is written as current-host-only, so Universal Clipboard does not send it to other devices, and tagged with org.nspasteboard.ConcealedType, which clipboard-history apps that follow nspasteboard.org's conventions skip.
  2. Hand off the clearing. multipass records the pasteboard's change count, a number macOS increments every time anything new is copied, and starts a detached copy of itself whose only argument is that number.
  3. Clear only its own copy. Thirty seconds later the detached process clears the clipboard, but only when the change count has not moved, so a later copy of the user's own survives. The secret never has to stay in memory to make that decision.

The Objective-C calls are the program's first unsafe code, kept in src/clipboard.rs behind a safe interface. The binary does not link AppKit: the module loads it with dlopen the first time a command touches the clipboard, so every other command runs without AppKit in its process. AGENTS.md now counts Apple's system frameworks like the Rust standard library, so cargo tree still lists only multipass. Off macOS, --clip fails with an error.

cards.title: Review so far
cards.html:
• The first review, of 9e04e95, requested changes with one finding: the README said AppKit was trusted only for --clip, but the binary linked AppKit at load time, so every command loaded it.
  • The fix, in 76d60b8, loads AppKit with dlopen only when the clipboard is needed. At 969b95a, --help loads 112 images, against 110 at the base and 719 before the fix, and tests/startup.rs fails if AppKit comes back. The review of 969b95a is clean.
  • The three suggestions are in: the README says any app on the Mac can read the value until it clears, the line count is updated, and the refusal of otp --set --clip names the exact case.
  • The secret's path was checked: it never reaches argv, the environment, a log line or an error, and a failed clearer clears the clipboard at once instead of leaving the secret behind.

cards.title: Terms
cards.html:
• Pasteboard: AppKit's name for the clipboard. The general pasteboard is the one copy and paste use.
  • Change count: a number the pasteboard increments whenever its contents are replaced. Comparing it tells whether anything was copied since.
  • Clearer: the detached multipass __clear-clipboard <count> process that clears the clipboard after 30 seconds.
  • objc_msgSend: the C function every Objective-C method call goes through. Rust calls it directly, cast to each method's exact signature.

groups.title: The clipboard module
groups.kicker: Writing to the macOS pasteboard, marking the value, and clearing it later
intro: src/clipboard.rs is new and holds everything that touches the clipboard. Its public interface is two functions: copy, which the command line calls with the value, and clear_later, which the detached clearer runs.

The file has two halves. The top half is ordinary Rust: the 30-second constant, the hidden command's name, the decision to clear only when the change count is unchanged, and the code that starts the clearer. The bottom half, mod macos, wraps the Objective-C runtime. It loads AppKit by its absolute path with dlopen, once per process, then looks up AppKit classes by name and sends messages through objc_msgSend, so no binding crate is needed. A stub of the same module for other systems returns an error from Pasteboard::general, so --clip fails cleanly there.

checks.text: A test cannot use the real clipboard without replacing the user's copy, so the three tests create a private pasteboard with pasteboardWithUniqueName and take a lock so they run one at a time. The path from a real copy to the clearer wiping the general pasteboard is not covered by a test.

files.note: New. Copies a value to the clipboard with its two markings and starts a detached process that clears it after 30 seconds.

checks.text: When the clearer cannot start, copy clears the clipboard at once and returns an error that names no value, so a failure never leaves the secret behind and never prints it. Checked by reading every error string in the file.
Comparing only the change count is what keeps a later copy of the user's own. keeps_a_later_copy_of_your_own is the test that fails if this ever clears unconditionally.

The clearer is found with current_exe, not a PATH lookup, its only argument is the change count, and its stdio is null so command substitution such as $(multipass get x --clip) does not wait 30 seconds for it. Checked by running __clear-clipboard 0 in a release build: 30 seconds, exit 0, clipboard untouched.

On Apple silicon, calling objc_msgSend as a variadic function passes arguments in the wrong registers, so each send helper casts it to the method's exact signature. A wrong return type here is undefined behaviour, so each call site's type parameter must match the method's declared type.

AppKit is opened by its absolute system path, the handle and dlerror's message are both checked for null, and the error names only AppKit and the loader's reason. Checked with otool -L, which no longer lists AppKit, and with DYLD_PRINT_LIBRARIES, which shows AppKit loading only when a clipboard test runs.

prepareForNewContentsWithOptions: returns NSInteger and setString:forType: returns BOOL, read here as i8, and NSPasteboardContentsCurrentHostOnly is 1. Checked against AppKit's declarations; the three clipboard tests pass at this head.

files.note: New. Fails if a command that never touches the clipboard loads AppKit.

checks.text: It also asserts that libSystem appears in dyld's list, so it cannot pass just because dyld printed nothing.

groups.title: Command-line wiring
groups.kicker: The --clip flag, the hidden clearing command, and where the value goes
intro: src/main.rs parses the new flag and routes each value through one function, deliver, which either prints it as before or copies it and says so on stderr without showing it.

The parser accepts --clip anywhere on the command line, then attaches it to get, or to otp when it shows a code, and refuses it everywhere else, as it already does for --force and --field. Before any parsing, main checks for the hidden __clear-clipboard command, so the clearer never goes through the ordinary command table or --help.

files.note: Adds --clip to get and otp, the hidden clearing command, and deliver, which prints or copies a value.

checks.text: The clearer is this same binary started with __clear-clipboard <count>. The count is not a secret, so it is safe in argv, where ps shows it for 30 seconds.
otp x --set --clip is refused with --clip only applies to get, and to otp without --set or --clear, which names the exact case the user hit.
deliver never writes the value to stdout or stderr when clip is set; it prints only the 30-second notice. Checked by reading every caller: get and otp are the only two.

groups.title: Documentation and rules
groups.kicker: What the README promises users and what AGENTS.md now allows
intro: The README replaces its two | pbcopy examples with --clip, adds a paragraph on what the clipboard copy does and does not protect against, and drops "Clipboard" from the list of features not built yet. It also adds AppKit to the code a user trusts beyond this repository, and says multipass loads it only for --clip.

AGENTS.md adds one rule: Apple's system frameworks count like the standard library under the no-dependencies rule, src/clipboard.rs loads AppKit only when --clip needs it, and any new unsafe code goes in a module like it, with a comment on what each call requires of its arguments.

files.note: Documents --clip, and names AppKit among the code a user trusts.

checks.text: The claim that multipass loads AppKit only for --clip holds at this head: otool -L lists only libobjc and libSystem, and --help loads no AppKit image. The line count now reads 1,600, which matches the non-test code outside src/crypto.
The two markings keep the value off other devices and out of history apps that honor them. The paragraph now says that any app running on this Mac can still read the clipboard during the 30 seconds.

files.note: Counts Apple's system frameworks like the standard library, and keeps unsafe code in modules like src/clipboard.rs.
